## Why This Is Asked

This question tests deriving a pure bitwise predicate for a regular pattern without branches.

## Key Concepts
- XOR of adjacent bits flags changes
- Masking with 0x7FFFFFFF resolves MSB ambiguity
- 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and portability

## Code Example
```c
int hasAlternatingBits(uint32_t n) {
  uint32_t t = n ^ (n >> 1);
  return (t & 0x7FFFFFFF) == 0x7FFFFFFF;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend to 64-bit inputs?
- What tests would you add for edge cases (MSB variations)?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests the ability to implement a deterministic, branchless byte-level permutation on a 128-bit value, a common pattern in low-level data encoding and hash-like transformations.

## Key Concepts

- Byte slicing and reassembly
- Unrolled, fixed permutations
- Inlining and branchless bit-twiddling

## Code Example

```c
// P is a 16-element permutation of {0..15}, evaluated at compile time
uint128 permuteBytes128(uint128 x) {
  return ( (x >> (8*0)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[0]) |
         ( (x >> (8*1)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[1]) |
         ...
         ( (x >> (8*15)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[15]);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate the permutation with generic tests without codegen changes?
- How would you adapt to a runtime-permutation while preserving inlining performance?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of bitwise rotations, a common low-level operation, and handling edge cases when k wraps around 32 without using branches. It also demonstrates how to make shifts robust against k=0 or k=31.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation using shifts and OR
- Modulo wrapping using masking and two's complement tricks
- Avoiding undefined shifts for k=0

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateLeft32(n, k) {
  k = k & 31;
  return ((n << k) | (n >>> ((-k) & 31))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for rotateRight32?
- How would you test boundary cases with k=0 and k=31?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests the ability to implement a branchless, 64-bit rotate using masking and shifts—a fundamental low-level technique in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts
- 64-bit masking with &63 to constrain the rotation range
- Branchless rotation via (n >> r) | (n << (64 - r))
- Edge-case handling for k=0 without conditional branches

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateRight64(n, k) {
  const r = k & 63;
  return (n >>> r) | (n << ((64 - r) & 63));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to arbitrary word sizes (e.g., 32-bit or 128-bit)?
- What are the trade-offs between rotate left and rotate right operations?
- How would this implementation behave on architectures with native rotate instructions?
